title: Gujarat's Swaminarayan
hook: a scripture made of questions asked out loud in a village courtyard

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gujarat's Swaminarayan: how Nilkanth became Sahajanand Swami, and how the mantra Swaminarayan became his name. Did one of your hellos carry a blessing? Day one thousand four hundred two.

Evening in a village in Gujarat. A courtyard, a raised seat, a crowd sitting on the ground: farmers, merchants, robed sadhus, children at the edges. The teacher on the seat is Swaminarayan, and he does something a teacher doesn't always do. He invites questions. Someone asks a hard one. Why does the mind keep running back to the same old cravings, even after years of devotion? He answers. Someone else pushes back. He answers again. And off to one side, a few of his senior sadhus are listening very closely, because they're going to write this down. Today, a holy book that began as a conversation.
screen: `A COURTYARD AT EVENING.` → `SOMEONE ASKS A HARD ONE.` → `SOMEONE WRITES IT DOWN.`

segments.voice: The book is called the Vachanamrut. Followers hear the title as vachan, words, and amrut, the nectar of immortality: nectar in the form of words. Swaminarayan followers hold it as scripture: his own teaching, gathered from talks in Gadhada and other villages, each one headed with the place, the setting, even what he was wearing that evening. Start with its shape. This scripture doesn't arrive as one voice speaking. It arrives as dialogue. A devotee asks, Swaminarayan answers, and sometimes he turns it around and asks the room a question, waiting to see who can answer. Learning happens in public, and sometimes the room has no answer to give. Then the content. The questions are practical. How do you know if your devotion is real? What do you do with anger toward someone in your own community? Why does a person who has heard good teaching still not change? These are the questions people ask at a kitchen table, and here they're treated as worth a scripture. And last, the thread. Running through the answers is a picture that tradition calls ekantik dharma, a whole-hearted life held up by four things together: dharma, doing what's right; knowledge of the self as distinct from the body; detachment, vairagya; and bhakti, love for God. Not one of them alone. All four, leaning on each other like the legs of a cot. So a scripture of questions is also a scripture that trusts the people asking. The answers matter. So does the fact that someone was allowed to ask.
screen: `VACHANAMRUT — NECTAR IN WORDS` · `A SCRIPTURE THAT BEGINS AS DIALOGUE` · `KITCHEN-TABLE QUESTIONS` · `FOUR THINGS HELD TOGETHER`

segments.voice: Four legs of a cot, one at a time. Sit comfortably, and let a few breaths go by. Then give one breath to each of the four. Doing what's right: where did you do it this week? Knowing yourself as more than the body: notice the one who is noticing. Letting go: one thing you could hold more loosely. Love: one face, or, if you pray, God. Then ask, without judging: which leg feels steady today, and which one wobbles? Rest on the whole cot for the last few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, the Vachanamrut, his teaching kept as questions and answers from evening gatherings. Today's word.
Your line: Gujarat's Swaminarayan. Today, ask someone a real question about something they know well, and listen all the way to the end of the answer. Day one thousand four hundred two.

howItsDone: In Swaminarayan mandirs and homes, passages from the Vachanamrut are read aloud and explained at gatherings, and devotees study it together.

fork.setup: you're a devotee in the courtyard. years of devotion, and the old cravings still come back. what do you do?
fork.reveal: in the Vachanamrut, questions like this are asked in public, and the answers became scripture.

Confirm: the talks were delivered in Gadhada and other villages and compiled by senior sadhus (tradition names Gopalanand, Muktanand, Nityanand and Shukanand Swami; not named in the voice); each discourse's heading records place, setting and his clothing.
